title: Beruriah's reading (Berakhot 10a)
hook: she teaches her husband to pray not for sinners to die, but for sin to end
carry: end the sin, not the sinner

segments.voice: Yesterday both schools spoke the words of the living God. Your line was quote the other side first. Did you say the other side first? Day two hundred eighty-three.

A neighbor who is loud at night and rude in the hallway, maybe worse. Lying awake, it's easy to wish they'd just disappear. In the Talmud, even a great sage had that wish. Rabbi Meir had some thugs in his neighborhood who made his life hard. And he prayed that they would die. His wife overheard. Her name was Beruriah. And she corrected him, just by reading the verse more closely.
screen: `I WISH THEY'D DISAPPEAR.` → `RABBI MEIR'S NEIGHBORS.` → `HIS WIFE OVERHEARS.`

segments.voice: In this story Beruriah is the teacher. In tractate Berakhot, she asks her husband: what are you basing this on? He's thinking of a line from the Psalms: "Let sinners cease out of the earth." Beruriah looks closer at the Hebrew. The verse doesn't use chot'im, the usual word for sinners. It says chata'im, a word that can also mean sins. So the verse is asking for sins to end, not for sinners to die. Then she points to the rest of the verse: "and let the wicked be no more." If the sins end, she says, there won't be any more wicked people. They'll have changed. So pray for them to turn back, not to die. The Talmud says Rabbi Meir prayed for mercy for them, and they did turn back. That's a whole ethic in one reading. The problem is the harm, not the human being doing it. People can change, and her reading leaves room for that. It doesn't mean pretending the harm isn't real. Beruriah takes it seriously enough to want it gone. She just aims the prayer at the right target. And notice how she does it: not with a speech, but by reading the text more carefully than her husband had.
screen: `LET SINNERS CEASE?` · `READ CLOSER: SINS, NOT SINNERS.` · `THEN THE WICKED WILL BE NO MORE.` · `PRAY FOR THEM TO TURN.` · then, large: `END THE SIN, NOT THE SINNER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: aim at the harm. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who's hurting you or people you love. Notice what you wish on them. Don't judge the wish. Now try Beruriah's move. Separate the person from the harm. Name the harm clearly: the cruelty, the lying, the noise. If you pray, you can ask for that harm to end, and for them to change. If not, simply hold both: the harm must stop, and the person can still turn. The bell holds the time.
Beruriah. The scholar who read the Psalm as sins, not sinners, and taught her husband to pray for the harm to end, not for the people to die.
Your line: end the sin, not the sinner. Today, when someone wrongs you, wish for the wrong to stop, and leave the person room to change. Day two hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Beruriah's reading is taught as a model of praying for wrongdoers to change, and Psalm 104, which contains the verse, is recited on the new month and, in some communities, on Shabbat afternoons in winter.

notes: Berakhot 10a paraphrased. The Hebrew in the verse is chata'im; the plain sense is 'sinners' (as JPS 1917 translates) and Beruriah reads it as 'sins'. The script's 'a word that can also mean sins' simplifies the argument; a Keeper should check the explanation.
The second half of the verse ('and let the wicked be no more') is quoted from JPS 1917 in the voice; check wording.
Beruriah's rulings appear in the Tosefta and she is praised in Pesachim 62b; 'one of the very few women quoted by name' is a common description.
howItsDone: Psalm 104 (Barchi Nafshi) customs vary by community.
